new_statements.quote: Stress is phonemic, but is not written. Examples: kaná 'heavy' kána 'road' Tone is predictable by stress. The stressed syllable is either mid or high tone.
new_statements.citation: SIL-PNG. 2004 [Payne 1994]. Organised Phonology Data: Kamano-Kafe [kbq]. 4 pp.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 3 to an image. Section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' reads exactly: 'Stress is phonemic, but is not. Examples: kaná 'heavy' kána 'road' / Tone is predictable by stress. The stressed syllable is either mid or high tone.' Nothing else on stress in the 4-page sheet (syllable patterns, conventions, texts, bibliography). Header: Kamano-Kafe Language [KBQ], Kainantu, Eastern Highlands, Gorokan family, data checked by Audrey Payne 1994. Reading lexical (unpredictable) is the right fixed-list label for 'phonemic' stress with a final-vs-initial minimal pair and no rule; relation 'refines' is right because the catalog rule field is empty and there are no existing statements.
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Kamano has an empty rule field and no existing statements; this sheet supplies the type (contrastive/phonemic stress, pitch predictable from stress) and a minimal pair, so it adds detail rather than agreeing or contradicting.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive (phonemic) and not marked in the orthography; the minimal pair kaná 'heavy' vs kána 'road' shows final vs initial stress in a disyllable. Pitch is not independent: the stressed syllable carries mid or high tone, so tone is derivable from stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the sheet gives only the one minimal pair.
new_statements.identity_note: All works describe Kamano (Kamano-Kafe [kbq]) of the Kainantu and Henganofi sub-districts, Eastern Highlands. Drew 1963 (p. 13, fn. 3) says the language was studied 'in the village of Knampa [scanned reading], on the Goroka road, ten miles from Kainantu' over 2.5 years; Payne 1964 (p. 2) contrasts the 'Finintign [scanned reading] dialect' with 'the Knampa dialect' with respect to an initial short vowel, so both manuscripts describe the Kanampa-area variety. The OPD lists villages Barola, Ina'onka, Onerunka, Raipinka etc. and was checked by Payne (1994).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the empty catalog record and with Drew 1963: adds culminativity (one pertinent stress per phonological word) and the unstressability of the transition vowel; silent on where the stress falls. The cross-reference in Drew 1963 (p. 6) names this paper as the fuller treatment of vowels and co-occurrence, not of stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is given. The paper is a distribution statement (syllable patterns, clusters, co-occurrence restrictions); it says only that each phonological word carries exactly one 'pertinent' (primary) stress, that the syllable is the unit of stress placement, and that the transition vowel inside consonant clusters is never stressed. Its examples (tonára, pasára, kfí'nea, psí'nea) happen to show penultimate stress but no rule is stated.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record has an empty rule; Drew is the fullest source and supplies the type (contrastive stress, position varies among the first three syllables), the verb-penult default with morphological overrides, and alternating secondary stress. Consistent with the OPD (stress phonemic; pitch follows stress).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word has one 'pertinent' (primary) stress, realised by length and intensity and usually higher pitch; it is contrastive and may fall on the first, second or third syllable of the word (attested patterns on 2-4 syllable words: '-, -', '--, -'-, --', '---, -'--, --'-; e.g. nóya' 'fish', pasá' 'bamboo comb', nóyara 'fish', tonára 'shelter', keginá 'fence', nágisaro' 'specific arrow', konímenta, kokorénta 'specific sweet potato'). Verbs are the predictable subcase: pertinent stress on the penultimate syllable unless a stress-attracting morpheme is present, in which case that morpheme's syllable is stressed. Nouns keep their lexical stress under suffixation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'Non-pertinent stresses radiate on alternate syllables preceding and succeeding the pertinent stress. A stress preceding the pertinent stress tends to be as strong as the pertinent stress whereas a succeeding stress is much lighter and may be imperceptible but has the rhythm of alternate stress.' (pp. 6-7). Non-pertinent stress skips object-pronoun prefixes and the -ga- of future markers, giving a 'taut' pattern (p. 9-10).
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs: stress-attracting morphemes override the penult (tentative future -su-/-s-; 2sg, 1/2-3 dual and 1pl 'final pronouns' in medial verbs; imperative marker syllable; 3pl final pronoun stressed on the final syllable; the suffix -na 'but' takes final stress; hortatory forms irregular: 1st-person dual hortatory stressed on the first syllable, plural hortatory on the penult except for 'go') (pp. 8-9). Stress never falls on object-pronoun prefixes or on -ga- of the future tense (p. 9). Four- and five-syllable words with a '--' pattern are treated as two phonological words (p. 7); the plural pronoun suffix on initially stressed disyllables gives '--' (p. 7). Nouns with suffixes 'usually keep their pertinent stress.. However there is some fluctuation and I feel this needs more work' (p. 10). In descriptive phrases phrase stress can perturb the pitch and intensity of stress to an alternate syllable while length stays on the lexical syllable (p. 10); in nouns the interrogative suffix draws stress to the final syllable (p. 11).
